In 1914, twenty eight men sailed to Antarctica. Their ship was trapped, crushed, and sunk by the ice.
And every single one of them came home alive.
This is the story of Ernest Shackleton and the Endurance.
Shackleton had a huge plan. Be the first to walk across the entire continent of Antarctica.
In December 1914, his ship, the Endurance, left the last whaling station on South Georgia island.
On board were sailors, scientists, a photographer, sixty nine sled dogs, and one stowaway.
They sailed into the Weddell Sea, one of the iciest seas on Earth.
In January 1915, just one day from their landing spot, the ice closed in around the ship.
One sailor said she was stuck like an almond in a chocolate bar.
For nine months, the ship drifted with the ice.
The men played football on the ice and trained the dogs. In winter, the sun did not rise for months.
Then the ice began to squeeze.
The ship groaned and cracked. Her wooden beams bent like bows.
On October 27th, 1915, Shackleton gave the order. Abandon ship.
A month later, they watched the Endurance sink beneath the ice.
Now, twenty eight men were camping on a floating sheet of ice, far from any land.
They had three small lifeboats, a few thin tents, and whatever food they could save.
They hunted seals and penguins. When food ran low, they even had to eat the dogs.
For five months, they drifted on the ice.
In April 1916, the ice began to break apart right under their tents.
They jumped into the three lifeboats and rowed for their lives.
After seven freezing days at sea, they landed on Elephant Island.
It was the first solid ground they had stood on in 497 days.
But nobody would ever look for them there. Elephant Island was far from any shipping route.
So Shackleton made a decision. He would go and get help.
With five men, he sailed a tiny lifeboat, the James Caird, towards South Georgia.
It was thirteen hundred kilometres away, across the most dangerous ocean in the world.
Waves as tall as buildings. Ice coated the boat, and they chipped it off by hand.
The navigator, Frank Worsley, could only see the sun four times. He found the island anyway.
After sixteen days, they reached South Georgia. But they had landed on the wrong side.
The whaling station was on the other side, past mountains that no one had ever crossed.
So Shackleton, Worsley and Tom Crean walked across them. No map, no tent, and screws in their boots for grip.
As night fell, they slid down a mountain on a coiled rope, straight into the dark.
After thirty six hours, they heard the seven o'clock whistle of the whaling station.
They walked in filthy and bearded. The station manager knew Shackleton, but did not recognise him.
But the job was not done. Twenty two men were still waiting on Elephant Island.
Shackleton tried three times to reach them. Each time, the ice blocked his ship.
On the fourth try, aboard a small Chilean ship called the Yelcho, he made it.
On August 30th, 1916, he counted the men on the beach. Every single one was alive.
In 2022, explorers finally found the Endurance, three kilometres deep, still in one piece.
Her name was still there, on the back of the ship.
The ship was lost. But not a single one of her men.
